newsitem.title: UK: Shareholders press Railtrack on investment.
newsitem.headline: Shareholders press Railtrack on investment.

text.p: Shareholders at the first annual meeting of British railway infrastructure company Railtrack Plc on Wednesday called on the group to plan new investments in facilities to encourage new passenger and freight rail services.

Railtrack, privatised in a giant 1.93 billion stg float earlier this year, has many former or current rail workers and users among its shareholders and several used the meeting at London's Barbican Hall to voice concerns about future spending.
They sought assurances that the group would try to reopen for passenger services lines closed in recent decades and also asked Railtrack to support expansion of freight opportunities.
Engineering and production director Brian Mellitt told the audience of several hundred investors that "investment is at levels the railway has not been assured of before".

Commercial director Michael Howell said, in response to a question on freight, that company did wish to address the fact that "the vast majority of British freight traffic is going by road", and said that it had designated 100 locations on its national network as "strategic freight sites".
These sites, mainly trackside real estate under the control of Railtrack's property management arm, could only be disposed of with the consent of major freight operators, he added.

Chairman Bob Horton, dealing with a number of questions on the level and standard of maintenance on track, signals and associated infrastructure said shareholders should "be assured that finances will be there to carry out work in a timely manner" in problem areas like the approaches to London's Euston and its busy West Coast main line to Manchester and Glasgow.
A seven-to-eight year upgrade of this route is currently in its early stages, and is seen costing up to 900 million stg.
Philip Isgar, head of implementation for the project, told Reuters the first two contracts for modernisation works between London and Rugby should be placed by mid-1997.

These first "main works" contracts will be for full-scale improvements and ongoing maintenance management that also link in with future signalling systems currently being designed by two competing engineering consortia, Isgar explained.
Railtrack was also looking at how to integrate the programme of core infrastructure renewal with two possible service upgrades -- for passenger services and for freight -- he added.

The passenger upgrades, which could include the acquisition of new high-speed tilting trains, are being discusssed with the Office of Passenger Rail Franchising, which says it may build them in an upcoming franchise contract for the West Coast line.

Partly because the line's equipment is nearing the end of its economic life, the route has suffered in recent years and its longhaul services are now struggling to compete with cheap air links and the faster East Coast main line, run by Sea Containers Ltd, which also serves Scotland.
Opraf said in a statement on Wednesday that, if appropriate, it may also consult interested local authorities on details of the planned upgrade before it drafts the West Coast franchise.
Railtrack is also discussing opportunities to enhance the route for freight with the Department of Transport which is working with promoters of a new road-on-rail carriage method.
Preparing the line for this system, dubbed Piggyback, could include raising the loading clearances of all trunk trackways to allow the carriage of full-height road trailers on rail wagons.
Backers of Piggyback, who include industry and freight transport groups, see big volumes of national and intercontental trailers switching from congested motorways onto such services.

Once in place, these trains could then run south of London and on into mainland Europe through the Channel Tunnel, thus extending the reach of Europe's existing road/rail freight lines which now span Austria, Italy, Germany and France to the UK.
